\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S1-Q04, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=4, type=single, subtopic={Processes}, answer={C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: work, heat for monatomic gas process with pressure related to volume | steps: process equation P V^k; molar heat capacity C = Cv + R/(1 - k); Q = n C delta T; evaluate}]
One mole of an ideal monoatomic gas is enclosed in a chamber at 300 K. The gas undergoes a process in which pressure is proportional to the volume. At the end of the process, the volume of the gas is doubled. The change in the internal energy of the gas is [$R$ is gas constant]
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{450 $R$}
\opt{B}{700 $R$}
\opt{C}{1350 $R$}
\opt{D}{data insufficient}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S3-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=5, type=numerical, subtopic={Processes}, answer={5}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: heat absorbed by gas, process P proportional to T to the one half | steps: process equation gives V proportional to T^(1/2); work = integral P dV; dU; Q = dU + W}]
One mole of an ideal monoatomic gas is taken from state A to state B through the process $P=\dfrac32T^{1/2}$. It is found that its temperature increases by 100 K in this process. Now it is taken from state B to C through a process for which internal energy is related to volume as $U=\dfrac12V^{1/2}$. The total work performed by the gas (in Joule) is $W$, if it is given that volume at B is 100 m$^3$ and at C it is 1600 m$^3$. [Use $R=8.3$ J/mol-K]. Fill $W/87$.
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P1-PHY-S2-Q12, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=1, qno=12, type=multi, subtopic={First law}, answer={A,B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: work, heat for a gas in a piston with spring or process | steps: Cv and R give gamma; first law and process equation; compute work, heat; check options}]
A piston-cylinder contains 1 kg of ideal gas with $C_V=615$ J/Kgk and $R=410$ J/Kgk. The initial pressure of the gas is $P_1=200$ kPa. The piston-cylinder also contains a metal block (in compressible). The block has mass 2 kg and specific heat capacity $C_b=305$ J/kgk. The block and gas is initially at 300 K. Assume no heat transfer to/from the cylinder/piston. The piston is pushed until temperature of gas reaches 363 K. The process happens rapidly so that there is no heat transfer between the gas and the block of metal. The piston is then locked in place and the gas and block come to thermal equilibrium over time. (Take : $1.1^5=1.61$)
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The pressure of the gas just after the rapid compression is 322 kPa}
\opt{B}{The final temperature of the block is close to 332 K}
\opt{C}{The final pressure of the gas is 221 kPa}
\opt{D}{Work done to push the piston is proportional to the molar mass of the gas.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P2-PHY-S1-Q06, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=2, qno=6, type=single, subtopic={Processes}, answer={C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=3, diff_parts={K1 S1 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: constant for an adiabatic process of an ideal gas | steps: a = P V^gamma; compute from given pressure and volume}]

Evaluate ``a constant'' for an adiabatic process involving exactly 10.0 mol of an ideal gas passing through the state having exactly $P=1.0$ atm and $T=1200$ K. \begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{4000 SI units}
\opt{B}{10000 SI units}
\opt{C}{100000 SI units}
\opt{D}{40000 SI units}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

A thermally insulating cylinder has a thermally insulating and frictionless movable partition in the middle, as shown in the figure below. On each side of the partition, there is one mole of an ideal gas, with specific heat at constant volume, $C_v=2R$. Here, $R$ is the gas constant. Initially, each side has a volume $V_0$ and temperature $T_0$. The left side has an electric heater, which is turned on at very low power to transfer heat $Q$ to the gas on the left side. As a result the partition moves slowly towards the right reducing the right side volume to $V_0/2$. Consequently, the gas temperatures on the left and the right sides become $T_L$ and $T_R$, respectively. Ignore the changes in the temperatures of the cylinder, heater and the partition.
\bfig{156.5}{SI09_p2_phy_s2_para9_10_1.png}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI11-P1-PHY-S3-Q04, source={Score-I - Test 11 (27 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=4, type=numerical, subtopic={Processes}, answer={1.77 to 1.79}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: ratio of work in isothermal and adiabatic expansion of helium | steps: W_iso = R T ln 4; temperature after adiabatic expansion by T V^(2/3) constant; W_adia = (3/2) R (T - T/4); ratio f ln2 | I: compute temperature drop in the adiabatic leg}]
Consider one mole of helium gas enclosed in a container at initial pressure $P_1$ and volume $V_1$. It expands isothermally to volume $4V_1$. After this, the gas expands adiabatically and its volume becomes $32V_1$. The work done by the gas during isothermal and adiabatic expansion processes are $W_{\text{iso}}$ and $W_{\text{adia}}$, respectively. If the ratio $\dfrac{W_{\text{iso}}}{W_{\text{adia}}}=f\ln2$, then $f$ is \underline{\hspace{1.5cm}}. -
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI11-P2-PHY-S2-Q01, source={Score-I - Test 11 (27 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=1, type=numerical, subtopic={Processes}, answer={2.05}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: bulk modulus of a bubble compressed isothermally | steps: pressure rise from Boyle's law for small a; pressure inside the bubble and surface tension term; bulk modulus definition; evaluate}]
A spherical bubble inside water has radius $R$. Take the pressure inside the bubble and the water pressure to be $p_0$. The bubble now gets compressed radially in an adiabatic manner so that its radius becomes ($R-a$). For $a\ll R$ the magnitude of the work done in the process is given by $(4\pi p_0Ra^2)X$, where $X$ is a constant and $\gamma=C_p/C_V=41/30$. The value of $X$ is \underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}.
\end{bankq}

A thermally isolated cylindrical closed vessel of height 8 m is kept vertically. It is divided into two equal parts by a diathermic (perfect thermal conductor) frictionless partition of mass 8.3 kg. Thus the partition is held initially at a distance of 4 m from the top, as shown in the schematic figure below. Each of the two parts of the vessel contains 0.1 mole of an ideal gas at temperature 300 K. The partition is now released and moves without any gas leaking from one part of the vessel to the other. When equilibrium is reached, the distance of the partition from the top (in m) will be \underline{\hspace{1.2cm}} (take the acceleration due to gravity $=10$ ms$^{-2}$ and the universal gas constant $=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$).
\bfig{62.7}{SI11_p2_phy_s3_q06_1.png}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SA24-P1-PHY-S2-Q08, source={Score Advanced - Test 24 (17 Apr 2024)}, paper=1, qno=8, type=single, subtopic={Processes}, answer={A}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S3 I1 C2 F0}, diff_note={concepts: molar heat capacity  process equation P = P0 + alpha/V | steps: find T = PV/R; dT/dV; work P dV; dQ = Cv dT + P dV; molar heat capacity C = Cv + P dV/dT; express; compute at a given volume | C: evaluating molar heat capacity for a non polytropic process}]
One mole of an ideal gas whose adiabatic exponent equals $\gamma$ undergoes a process $P=P_0+\alpha/v$, where $P_0$ and $\alpha$ are positive constants. Its volume increases from $v_1$ to $v_2$.\par
{\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{1.5pt}\noindent\begin{tabular}{|c|L{3.0cm}|c|L{3.2cm}|} \hline & \multicolumn{1}{c|}{List-I} & & \multicolumn{1}{c|}{List-II}\\ \hline
(I) & Heat capacity of gas as a function of its volume & (P) & $\dfrac{P_0(V_2-V_1)}{\gamma-1}$\\ \hline
(II) & Internal energy increment of a gas & (Q) & $\dfrac{P_0(V_2-V_1)}{\gamma-1}+\alpha\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$\\ \hline
(III) & The work performed by it & (R) & $P_0(V_2-V_1)+\alpha\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$\\ \hline
(IV) & The amount of heat transferred & (S) & $\dfrac{\gamma R}{\gamma-1}+\dfrac{\alpha R}{p_0v}$\\ \hline
\end{tabular}}\par
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{I $\rightarrow$ S;II $\rightarrow$ P;III $\rightarrow$ R;IV $\rightarrow$ Q}
\opt{B}{I $\rightarrow$ P;II $\rightarrow$ Q;III $\rightarrow$ R;IV $\rightarrow$ S}
\opt{C}{I $\rightarrow$ P;II $\rightarrow$ S;III $\rightarrow$ R;IV $\rightarrow$ Q}
\opt{D}{I $\rightarrow$ S;II $\rightarrow$ P;III $\rightarrow$ Q;IV $\rightarrow$ S}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SA25-P1-PHY-S2-Q07, source={Score Advanced - Test 25 (21 Apr 2024)}, paper=1, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={First law}, answer={A,B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K1 S3 I1 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: gas escaping  a thermally insulated cylinder through a valve | steps: work done by the piston pushing gas out; internal energy and enthalpy balance; final temperature of the leaving gas; speed of outflow; adiabatic expansion; check | C: open system energy balance for gas escaping through a hole}, also_in={Score Advanced - Test 26 (21 Apr 2024) P1 Q7}]
At the end of the thermally insulated cylinder with the piston there is a valve (figure) that covers a small hole, which opens and begins to let air from outside into the cylinder at a pressure difference $\Delta P=P_0/3$ ($P_0$ is atmospheric pressure). The valve does not allow air to escape from the cylinder to the outside. At the initial moment of time, the piston is pressed against the end of the cylinder, there is no air inside.\par
In the first case, the cylinder is filled with air to volume $V_0$, slowly moving the piston, after which it is stopped, and then the piston is released.\par
In the second case, the piston is abruptly moved to a position in which the volume under the piston is equal to $V_0$, so that the air does not have time to penetrate through the valve into the cylinder. In this position, fix the piston, wait until the cylinder is filled with air, just as in the first case, release the piston. Out side the cylinder is air at atmospheric pressure $P_0$ and temperature $T_0$. The friction of the piston against the walls, the mass of the piston, as well as the heat exchange of air with the piston and the cylinder walls can be neglected. Air can be considered a diatomic ideal gas. After the piston is released, the valve remains closed all the time.\par
\bfig{56.0}{SA25_p1_phy_s2_q06_2.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{For first case the temperature of air inside the cylinder at the moment the piston is stopped at volume $V_0$ is $T_0$.}
\opt{B}{For first case, the temperature of air inside the cylinder when the piston stops movement is $\dfrac87T_0$.}
\opt{C}{For second case, the temperature of the air in the cylinder after stopping of piston and filling with air is $\dfrac75T_0$.}
\opt{D}{For second case, the temperature of the air after piston is released and it stops movement is $\dfrac95T_0$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

Now, a heater H is switched on which supplies heat slowly to one of the chambers. Heater is kept on till the partition S$_2$ moves through the quarter of the circle. At this position the heater is switched off and the partition S$_2$ remains in equilibrium. Neglect any friction as well as heat loss to the surrounding through the walls of the tube. Consider one mole of helium gas enclosed in a container at initial pressure $P_1$ and volume $V_1$. It expands isothermally to volume $4V_1$. After this, the gas expands adiabatically and its volume becomes $32V_1$. The work done by the gas during isothermal and adiabatic expansion processes are $W_{\text{iso}}$ and $W_{\text{adia}}$, respectively. If the ratio $\dfrac{W_{\text{iso}}}{W_{\text{adia}}}=f\ln2$, then $f$ is \underline{\hspace{2cm}}.
\end{bankq}

A thermally isolated cylindrical closed vessel of height $8$ m is kept vertically. It is divided into two equal parts by a diathermic (perfect thermal conductor) frictionless partition of mass $8.3$ kg. Thus the partition is held initially at a distance of $4$ m from the top, as shown in the schematic figure below. Each of the two parts of the vessel contains $0.1$ mole of an ideal gas at temperature $300$ K. The partition is now released and moves without any gas leaking from one part of the vessel to the other. When equilibrium is reached, the distance of the partition from the top (in m) will be \underline{\hspace{2cm}}\\
(take the acceleration due to gravity $=10$ ms$^{-2}$ and the universal gas constant $=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$).

\begin{bankpassage}[id=JA03-P2-PHY-S2-G11-12, source={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 03 (01 Mar 2021)}, questions={11-12}]
From first law of thermodynamics, if some quantity of heat ($Q$) is supplied to a system capable of doing external work ($W$), then the quantity of heat absorbed by the system is equal to the sum of the increase in internal energy ($\Delta U$) of the system and the work done by the system
\[Q=W+\Delta U\]
Also for an ideal gas $\Delta U=\dfrac f2nR\Delta T$ where $\Delta T$ : increase in temp and $f$ : degree of freedom, Work done by force $W=\int\vec F\cdot d\vec s$, work done by gas $=\int p\cdot dv$ and gravitational potential energy $=mgh$. Take $R=\dfrac{25}3$ J / mol $-$ K, $g=10$ m/s$^2$
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=JA11-P2-PHY-S3-G17-18, source={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 11 (20 May 2021)}, questions={17-18}]
\textbf{Air Standard Otto cycle :}\\
The air-standard-Otto cycle is the ideallzed cycle for the spark-ignition internal combustion engines. This cycle is shown on P-V and T-S diagrams. The Otto cycle 1-2-3-4 consists of following four process:\\
Process 1-2: Reversible adiabatic compression of air.\\
Process 2-3: Heat addition at constant volume.\\
Process 3-4: Reversible adiabatic expansion of air.\\
Process 4-1: Heat rejection at constant volume.
\bfig{123.5}{JA11_p2_phy_s3_para17_18_1.png}
Mean Effective Pressure is defined as the ratio of the net work done to the displacement volume of the piston.
\end{bankpassage}
\begin{bankq}[id=JA11-P2-PHY-S3-Q17, source={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 11 (20 May 2021)}, paper=2, qno=17, type=single, subtopic={Heat engines}, answer={A}, answer_src=key, difficulty=2, diff_parts={K1 S2 I0 C0 F0}, diff_note={concepts: adiabatic relations in an Otto cycle | steps: heat in and out occur at constant volume; use T V^(gamma - 1) = constant for the adiabatic steps; efficiency is 1 - (T4 - T1)/(T3 - T2) = 1 - (1/r)^(gamma - 1)}, group=JA11-P2-PHY-S3-G17-18]

Then the efficiency of the cycle is given as.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\eta_{th}=1-\left(\dfrac1r\right)^{\gamma-1}$}
\opt{B}{$\eta_{th}=1+\left(\dfrac1r\right)^{\gamma-1}$}
\opt{C}{$\eta_{th}=1+\left(\dfrac1r\right)^{\gamma+1}$}
\opt{D}{$\eta_{th}=1-\left(\dfrac1r\right)^{\gamma+1}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=JA11-P2-PHY-S3-Q18, source={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 11 (20 May 2021)}, paper=2, qno=18, type=single, subtopic={Heat engines}, answer={A}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C0 F0}, diff_note={concepts: net work of an Otto cycle, ideal gas equation of state | steps: net work is C_v[(T3 - T2) - (T4 - T1)]; C_v = R/(gamma - 1); express R using P1 V1/T1; divide by the displacement volume V1 - V2 = V1(r - 1)/r to get the mean pressure | I: write n R as P1 V1/T1 to convert the work into the pressure form}, group=JA11-P2-PHY-S3-G17-18]

\opt{B}{$\left(\dfrac1{\gamma+1}\right)\left(\dfrac{P_1}{T_1}\right)\left(\dfrac r{r-1}\right)\big\{(T_3-T_2)+(T_4-T_1)\big\}$}
\opt{C}{$\left(\dfrac1{\gamma-1}\right)\left(\dfrac{P_1}{T_1}\right)\left(\dfrac r{r+1}\right)\big\{(T_3-T_2)+(T_4-T_1)\big\}$}
\opt{D}{$\left(\dfrac1{\gamma-1}\right)\left(\dfrac{P_1}{T_1}\right)\left(\dfrac r{r-1}\right)\big\{(T_3+T_2)+(T_4-T_1)\big\}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=JA13-P1-PHY-S1-Q01, source={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 13 (31 May 2021)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=multi, subtopic={Heat pumps}, answer={A,B,C}, answer_src=key, working={Heat removed rate cannot exceed the Carnot value P T\_L/(T\_H - T\_L), so A B C may occur.}, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: coefficient of performance of an ideal refrigerator | steps: COP of a Carnot cycle run in reverse is T_L/(T_H - T_L); heat removed per work is at most this value; rate of heat removal is P times COP at most; options not above the Carnot bound are possible | I: the phrase 'may be' means any value up to the Carnot limit}]
A room air conditioner is modelled as a heat engine run in reverse. An amount of heat $Q_{in}$ is absorbed from the room at a temperature $T_L$ by the cooling coils which contains a working gas; this gas is compressed adiabatically to a temperature $T_H$; then the gas is compressed isothermally in a coil outside of the house, giving off an amount of heat $Q_{out}$; the gas expands adiabatically back to a temperature $T_L$ and finally expanded isothermally to original state and the cycle is repeated. An amount of energy $W$ is input into the system in every cycle through an electric pump. This model describes the air conditioner with the best possible efficiency.
\bfig{158.2}{JA13_p1_phy_s1_q01_1.png}
The outside air temperature is $T_H$ and the inside air temperature is $T_L$. The air conditioner unit consumes electric power $P$. Assume that the air is dry sufficiently so that no condensation of water occurs in the cooling coils of the air conditioner. Which of the following may be the rate at which heat is removed from the room?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\dfrac P2\left(\dfrac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}\right)$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{3P}4\left(\dfrac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}\right)$}
\opt{C}{$P\left(\dfrac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}\right)$}
\opt{D}{$\dfrac{3P}2\left(\dfrac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}\right)$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=JA15-P2-PHY-S3-G3-4, source={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 15 (12 Jun 2021)}, questions={3-4}]
Air Standard Otto cycle :\\
The air-standard-Otto cycle is the ideallzed cycle for the spark-ignition internal combustion engines. This cycle is shown on P-V and T-S diagrams. The Otto cycle 1-2-3-4 consists of following four process:\\
Process 1-2: Reversible adiabatic compression of air.\\
Process 2-3: Heat addition at constant volume.\\
Process 3-4: Reversible adiabatic expansion of air.\\
Process 4-1: Heat rejection at constant volume.
\bmissing{p2_phy_s3_para3_4_1}
Mean Effective Pressure is defined as the ratio of the net work done to the displacement volume of the piston.
\end{bankpassage}

\end{tabular}}

Assume that all work produced by running engines can be stored and used without dissipation.

\opt{B}{The minimum  temperature $T_2$ to which the first object can be lowered is 250 K.}
